If you say that making a vow to seek rebirth in the Pure Land and to be received by the Buddha’s guidance must necessarily be the work of Māra, then [what about] the Buddha..."
This leads people astray into the palace of Māra! When Samantabhadra instructed others to make vows, he said: "May I, when my life is about to end, behold that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face.
How could the writings of Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna and the sages and worthies of successive generations all cause people to go mad and wish to be born in the palace of Māra?
For you to make such a claim is to sever the seeds of the Buddha; what is this other than Māra himself?
(Regarding the Pure Land, the Mara and the Buddha may be contrasted).
Master Lingzhi Zhaolüshi said: "The *Amitābha Sūtra*’s instruction on reciting the Buddha’s name sets a time limit of one day or seven days according to the practitioner’s commitment;
however, the principle must necessarily rely upon the *Contemplation Sūtra*, the 'Great Text,' which has no fixed limit for days, extending down to even ten recitations."
To achieve rebirth through the cultivation of pure karma, one must first collect the mind and face the west with palms joined and body upright.

One should contemplate from afar that Buddha currently seated at the site of enlightenment, together with his environment and its adornments, his radiance, and his marks and signs of excellence. One should then lament for oneself:
"This body of mine has long been submerged in the ocean of suffering, drifting through birth and death, solitary and without refuge, like an infant fallen into a pit."
Crying out to one's parents for urgent rescue from perilous death, one single-mindedly relies upon [the Buddha] and earnestly seeks liberation;

with every sound continuous and every thought unwavering, although later the affairs and practices may differ and the states of mind be either concentrated or distracted, all constitute pure karma and one shall fully attain rebirth.
Otherwise, they would merely be indeterminate conditions of delusion, resulting only in empty blessings (from the *Amitābha Sūtra Commentary*).
Question: The *Contemplation Sūtra* states, "This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. Since the mind is already the Buddha, why is it necessary to recollect another Buddha? Answer:
It is precisely because the mind is fundamentally the Buddha that one now single-mindedly recollects that Buddha. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra Precepts* state:

"One must always know for oneself that I am a Buddha who has not yet attained completion, whereas the Buddhas are those who have already attained completion. Your own mind is the Buddha. This refers to the Buddha within your own mind.
One who has not yet attained Buddhahood is like Amitābha Buddha, who has already attained it.

A Buddha-to-be has long been submerged in the ocean of desire, fully possessed of afflictions, with no foreseeable time for escape; a Buddha who has already attained it has long realized Bodhi, is fully endowed with majestic power and divinity, and is able to protect all beings.
Therefore, the various sutras exhort one to practice mindfulness of the Buddha; this is precisely seeking help from another because one has not yet attained Buddhahood oneself.

It is precisely because he has already attained Buddhahood that he acts as a protector; therefore, if sentient beings do not mindfully recollect the Buddha, the holy and the mundane will be forever separated, fathers and sons will drift apart, and they will dwell long in saṃsāra, remaining far removed from the Buddha.
Ordinary beings on the stage of thinness, bound by karma and afflictions, transmigrate through the five realms for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas;

yet if they suddenly hear of the Pure Land and resolve to seek rebirth there, reciting the Name for even a single day, they shall immediately transcend to that land, be protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas, and proceed directly toward Bodhi.

This may be called a rare encounter difficult to meet in ten thousand kalpas, occurring but once in a thousand lifetimes. I vow that from this day forth until the end of the future, wherever I may be, [I shall practice accordingly].
The praise of these manifold exhortations and inducements, the resulting lands and bodies, and the karmic conditions of those to be transformed are no different from those of Amitābha Buddha;
this heart’s boundless gratitude can only be witnessed by the Buddha.
Chan Master Changlu Ze said: "The people of this land do not fail to loathe the clamor and vexation of the secular home and admire the tranquility of the *ārāma* (monastery).

Therefore, they abandon their homes and leave the household life, praising it with great earnestness. Yet, the manifold sufferings of *Sahā* [this world] are far more than the clamor and vexation of the secular home;
the ease and leisure of *Sukhāvatī* [the Land of Utmost Bliss] are by no means merely the tranquility of the *ārāma*. One must know how to transcend..."

To find beauty in one's own home while having no desire to be reborn there is the first delusion. Those who labor for ten thousand miles to seek out spiritual teachers do so entirely to illuminate the Great Matter and resolve the questions of life and death;

yet the World-Honored One Amitābha possesses a supreme karma of form and mind, and his power of great vows is vast and profound—when he utters his single perfect voice, nothing is not clearly in accord with their aspirations. Thus, they wish to attend upon a teacher but have no desire to see [Amitābha].

To be deluded regarding these two matters is the second error. To delight in dwelling within vast monastic communities while having no desire to rely upon the sites of practice for those with few followers;

and yet, to wish to draw near to such communities while not admiring the pure assembly of the Western Pure Land, where those in their final birth before Buddhahood are exceedingly numerous and all the supreme virtuous ones gather in one place—this is the third error. This...

Compared to those in this world, where the longest lifespan does not exceed a hundred years, and where childhood ignorance, senility, decrepitude, and disease follow one another in succession, while dullness and sleep constantly prevail—
even though the Bodhisattvas remain obscured by the "intermediate state" (*antarābhava*) and the Śrāvakas are still ignorant until they emerge from the womb—
the people of the Western Land lose nine-tenths of every fleeting moment before reaching the stage of non-retrogression; this is truly enough to cause one’s heart to tremble with cold.

Their lifespan is immeasurable; once they have entrusted themselves to the lotus calyx, they shall never again suffer the pain of death, continuing in an uninterrupted succession until they reach Bodhi.
Thus, they immediately attain the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), and their certainty is predictable.

While those who wander through the Sahā world are deluded by its fleeting shadows, those in the Pure Land enjoy long years. This is the fourth delusion. As for those whose rank is non-retrogressive and whose fruit is realized as such—

Born in the realm of desire yet free from desire, dwelling amidst the dust of the world yet untainted by it, one is then able to give rise to unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*) and exercise the sorrow for all beings as one’s own body.
Returning to the toils of the mundane world, one blends with the light amidst the five turbidities.

Yet there are those of shallow learning and meager wisdom who, upon attaining a slight degree of goodness, claim to have forever emerged from the four currents of existence and transcended the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). They revile the Pure Land while remaining attached to this Sahā world, thus closing their eyes to the void.

To return [to one's home] while wandering aimlessly alongside oxen and horses, following in their tracks to the *niraya* hells without knowing who one is, and yet to compare oneself to the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta—this is the fifth delusion.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "One should make a vow, vowing to be born in that land.
To disbelieve the sincere words of the Buddhas and not wish to be born in the Pure Land—is this not most profound delusion? (Weijiang ji)

When one’s parents come to believe and know that it is the time to plant the lotus of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), they should single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name; this is the time when the lotus emerges from the water.

A filial son, perceiving that the moment of their parents’ rebirth has arrived, should compile their various merits throughout their lives into a single document and read it to them from time to time to inspire joy.
Furthermore, he should request his parents to sit or lie facing west, never forgetting to do so.

In the Pure Land, one should set up an image of Amitābha, burn incense, strike the chime, and chant the Buddha’s name without ceasing. At the time of casting off this life, one must further apply focused intent;
do not lose right mindfulness through weeping and wailing. That one’s parents may attain birth in the Pure Land and receive all manner of bliss—how magnificent would that not be!
The filial care provided throughout one’s life finds its true fulfillment at this very moment. I entrust these words to filial sons and obedient grandsons: do not forget them.
Regarding this matter:
recollecting the Buddha does not obstruct the practice of Chan, and practicing Chan does not obstruct the recollection of the Buddha. Although these are two gates, their principle is identical.
Those of superior wisdom, in all their activities, do not cling to these two truths; those of inferior wisdom each establish themselves in one side alone.

Therefore, when they do not harmonize, much contention arises; thus, those who practice Chan (Zen) disparage the recitation of the Buddha’s name, while those who recite the Buddha’s name disparage the practice of Chan.

Both stem from clinging to the ultimate as real and slandering the provisional, or clinging to the provisional as real and slandering the ultimate. Since neither has yet realized the fruit of the Path, they first distinguish themselves for rebirth in hell.

One must know that the capacities of practitioners vary in depth and shallowness, so that each may obtain what is appropriate for them. For example, how could a farmer tending his fields possibly open a treasury?

How can those who open the treasury be expected to manage agricultural fields? If one were to have those who manage fields open the treasury, it would be like a lame person attempting to climb a mountain;
if one were to have those who open the treasury manage fields, it would be like forcing a noble person into a lowly station. In the end, neither would succeed.

It is better for those who manage fields to simply manage their own fields, and for those who open the treasury to simply open the treasury; let each follow what they prefer, and all will attain success.

Since the mind is thus, those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and those who engage in Zen meditation each seek their own fundamental principle; though the streams and mountains differ, the clouds and moon are the same.
One may truly say that at every place the green willows can tether the horse, and at every household the gate leads straight to Chang'an.
Huìjué asked Master Yù: "Some say that the Pure Land is merely a skillful means (*upāya*) of the Sage to accommodate those of dull faculties and transform ordinary vessels.
If one could transcend directly and enter the stage of a Tathāgata all at once, what need would there be for 'other power' (*parāśakti*)?
He replied: "In the Buddha’s lifetime, there were Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra; after his passing, there were Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna; and in this land, there were Zhìzhě and Zhìjué."

If all those who vow to be reborn in the Pure Land must necessarily be of dull faculties, then when Śākyamuni exhorted his father, King Śuddhodana, and the sixty thousand members of the Śākya clan to likewise vow for rebirth in the Pure Land, were they all merely ordinary vessels?

Should these sages and worthies all fall short of the sharp faculties and superior capacities found in people today? Moreover, if this is taken as a provisional teaching, what then constitutes the ultimate reality?

The distinction between the provisional and the ultimate is not limited to a single path; were it not for one with the "eye of the teachings" clearly open, how could one discern them? I address you, O wise ones:
you must believe the Buddha’s words that the retribution [for transgressions] is no light matter; do not treat this with casual ease (as seen in the *Lèbāng wénlèi*).
Chan Master Sixin Xin said: "For those who practice Chan, it is best to recite the Buddha's name.

If one’s faculties are dull and fear that they may not attain great enlightenment in this life, they should rely on the power of Amitābha’s vows to be guided to rebirth in the Pure Land. It is like being under the protection of an official’s patronage;

one need not worry about failing the examinations, for rank and emolument are already assured. There is a certain class of people who say, 'My mind is inherently good, so there is no need to recite. "
O Buddha, let me ask you: where does your benevolence reside? You rejoice when praised, yet you grow angry when reviled.
Such perverse views delude and confuse the people of the world. I exhort all persons:

throughout the twelve periods of the day, regardless of public or private affairs, whether attending to official business, managing domestic matters, or receiving guests, you must find stillness amidst busyness and steal moments of leisure within the clamor. Keep this in mind and recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. Or...
Reciting the name a hundred times, a thousand times, or ten thousand times as one’s daily practice, and maintaining this throughout one’s entire life, one will be reborn in that land.
If you do not believe the Buddha’s words, what words can be believed? If you are not reborn in the Pure Land, in what land could you be reborn?
If you do not awaken with urgency, how far will you be driven by the waves of worldly toil before you reach the ultimate end? (From *The Exhortation to Practice the Pure Land*)
Master Wén said: "In general, those who practice the path of Pure Land must skillfully resolve their aspiration (*cittotpāda*).

If one does so out of personal aversion for the five turbidities and longing for the nine grades of rebirth, this contradicts the bodhicitta; such is the practice of a *śrāvaka* and should not be resolved upon.

If, however, one gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) for the sake of sentient beings, seeking to go to that land and hoping to quickly achieve the power of the Way and spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*) to travel throughout the ten directions—"
To rescue and deliver all beings so that they may together attain the Buddha-way is to accord with the bodhicitta;
this is the practice of a bodhisattva which one should resolve to undertake. (The Dharma-gate of Pure Conduct)

Repentance is like diligently polishing an ancient mirror, gradually eradicating the accumulated dust of generations; mindfulness of the Buddha is like privately encountering an enlightened sovereign, suddenly attaining future deliverance.

Within the four seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—and amidst every movement of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, one should earnestly contemplate the adornments of the Pure Land and constantly keep Amitābha Buddha in mind.
If one acts thus, the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha will manifest.
Formerly, Chan Master Feixi of Caotang said: "One who bathes in the great ocean has already utilized the waters of the hundred rivers;
likewise, one who recites the Buddha's name will surely achieve samādhi. It is just as when a clear pearl is dropped into turbid water—the turbid water cannot [obstruct it]."

If one does not maintain the perception of the Buddha while casting [the mind] into a distracted state, the distracted mind cannot fail to become the Buddha. Once this accord is achieved, both mind and Buddha vanish;
when both mind and Buddha have vanished, then all myriad conditions and all sensory objects are nothing other than samādhi (from the *Bao Wang Lun*).
People of the world mostly take gems, jade, crystal, diamond, bodhi seeds, or wood from the *mukha* tree to make prayer beads (*japamālā*).
I, however, take the inhalation and exhalation of breath as my prayer beads; I recite the Buddha’s name following the breath. Having great reliance upon this, I am at peace even in the face of fear.

Is there anyone who, having failed to complete even a single breath, belongs to the next life? Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, I constantly employ these beads. Even when... [the text continues].
When you fall asleep, let your mind dwell upon the Buddha; as soon as you awaken, continue this practice.
You will surely behold that Buddha within your dreams, just as smoke rising before the appearance of fire when drilling for a spark. If you do not cease this dreaming, samādhi will be accomplished.
To face the Buddha’s jade-white brow and receive his personal prediction of enlightenment is something that will certainly happen without fail.
Chan Master Zhenxie Le said: "The lineage of the Dongshan school all devotes itself to secret cultivation; what is the reason for this?

It is because the path of practice in the Buddha-remembrance dharma-gate is directly based on the Great Canon to receive those of superior faculties, while also extending to lead those of middling and inferior capacities.
As the Sutra says: 'If a person hears the name of Amitābha Buddha and holds it in mind, whether for one day or more...'"
If one maintains single-mindedness without distraction for seven days, one will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
If one is a person of superior capacity, upon being prompted here, they should raise this thought and take a look; by seeing through it, what is the face of Amitābha Buddha, and what is his realm?
Would this not be a direct leap straight into the stage of the Tathāgata? Those of middling and inferior capacities rely entirely upon faith and aspiration.

Because mindfulness arises immediately upon being bound [to the object], the teaching of "single-mindedness without distraction" encompasses two meanings: the single mind of principle (*li-yixin*) and the single mind of phenomena (*shi-yixin*).
If it is the single mind of phenomena, this is the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*) that all people can practice; as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
"Recalling the Buddha and mindful of the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha in the present or the future, without depending on expedient means. It is self-evident.

This conveys the meaning of attaining the opening of the mind, which encompasses practitioners of both middle and lower capacities. That is to say: first, maintain mindfulness as a dragon finding water or a tiger relying on a mountain.
Regarding the principle of single-mindedness, it is not some other method; simply take the four characters "A-mi-t'o-fo" (Amitābha Buddha) as a firm *huatou* (critical phrase).
Throughout the six periods of the day and night, from the moment of the ten recitations at dawn, pull this up directly and continuously without interruption.
By means of the mind that does not contemplate through non-existence, nor through neither-existence-nor-non-existence, nor through both-existence-and-non-existence;
with the severance of the limits of past and future, such that not a single thought arises and one does not traverse the stages, but suddenly transcends to the Buddha-ground—
therefore, the ocean of practice is exhausted, the vows of Samantabhadra are fulfilled, and although the land of Amitābha Buddha is empty, it is precisely this that Vimalakīrti focused upon.
Cultivating faith in the Pure Land, one knows that whether in the teachings or in Chan, both Buddhas and patriarchs have all cultivated pure karma and returned to this single source.
Once one enters this gate, one is able to enter all infinite Dharma gates (the Pure Land teaching).

Question: Since every person inherently possesses the Pure Land of the Mind and the original nature of Amitābha, why do they not directly accept this as their own, instead seeking [the Buddha] ten million *koṭi* of lands away?
Answer: If one can realize that the Pure Land is within the mind and that Amitābha is one’s own original nature, what difficulty could there be in traveling ten million *koṭi* of lands?
Even lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges would not be considered far; how much less so these ten million *koṭi* of lands?
It is not heard that when the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra takes a single step within a single pore, he passes through unspeakably many worlds;
yet the pores do not narrow, nor do the worlds expand. Master Li said: "The ocean of boundless lands does not separate self and other at the tip of a hair;
the ten periods of past and present never depart from the present moment. Therefore, the World-Honored One Amitābha...
This is merely a direct pointing to the single Buddha within the mind;
it does not refer to the entire substance of the mind as the source from which "mind-only pure land," "mind-only hell," and "mind-only the six realms" arise. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"The empty space of the ten directions arises within your own mind, like a small cloud appearing amidst the great blue sky. It further states: "Space arises within the Great Awakening..."
The ocean is but a single bubble; how great is the mind! What dharma does it not encompass? Thus, the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
This is the place where the Patriarchs attained enlightenment; it does not fall within the realm of thought or deliberation, nor can it be grasped through conjecture.
To engage in such conceptual analysis is much like marking the spot on a boat to find a sword that has long since been lost. The sword is gone.
Question: Since this is the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), why point specifically toward the West? Answer:

Precisely because the Dharma-realm is perfectly interfused, every phenomenon does not depart from its own fundamental position. The Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) is omnipresent in all places; thus, to mention one is to encompass the whole.
It is like the thousand-jeweled net in the palace of Śakra, where the light and shadows of the thousand jewels all enter into a single jewel, and that single jewel [enters into all].
The light and shadows pervade all a thousand pearls; though each pearl mutually pervades the others, this pearl cannot become that pearl, and that pearl cannot become this one.
They interpenetrate without being confused, and though separated they are not divided. Each is fully manifest, yet there is no location where it dwells.
Amitābha’s Pure Land is but one of these thousand pearls, and among the ten million Buddha-lands, each individual Buddha-land likewise consists of a thousand pearls.
From those of the three vehicles up to the inhabitants of the hells and hungry ghosts—each and every one is none other than a single saint among the thousand beads.
Through the skillful means of the Sage, by single-mindedly recollecting Amitābha Buddha, one directly points to the single bead among the thousand.
To see this one Buddha is to see all Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as the sentient beings of the dharma-realm and the oceans of lands within atoms throughout the ten directions.
Throughout the ages, this single seal has been perfectly complete from the outset, leaving no further dharma to be attained.
The Vinaya Master Qingzhao Heng, upon hearing that Hu Xianyi was ill, slandered him by saying:
"In my entire life, I have been on good terms with Xianyi, yet we never once spoke of the final stroke—the great matter. How could he not know how to establish his own security and destiny?"
Xuanyi said, "It is said that if the mind is pure, the land is pure. The Master asked, "In the twelve periods of the day, have you ever had impure thoughts or defilements?
Xuanyi replied, "Since one dwells in the world, how can one avoid impure thoughts?
The Master said, "If this is so, then how can the mind be pure and the land be pure? (From the *Biography of Xuanyi Hu*).

Chan Master Tianyi Huai asked his students, "If one says that they abandon defilement to take up purity, or loathe this world while rejoicing in that, then such sentiments of acceptance and rejection are merely the deluded thoughts of sentient beings.
Yet, if one says there is no Pure Land, that contradicts the Buddha’s words.
Now, those who cultivate the Pure Land—how should they cultivate it? He then answered himself: "When born, one is certainly born; when departing, one truly departs."
(See Master Ne’s *Wen on the Pure Land of Mind-Only* for further details).
The Dharma Master Ying of Tongjiang wrote a "Discernment of the Two Modes of Emergence: Vertical and Horizontal," stating:

"As for vertical emergence, Śrāvakas cultivate the Four Noble Truths, Pratyekabuddhas cultivate the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and Bodhisattvas cultivate the Six Perfections and myriad practices; these involve the positions of others, and are thus likened to [a boat crossing a river]."
Passing the imperial examinations requires that one possess innate talent and learning; likewise, the successive promotion through official ranks requires that one have achieved merit and efficacy.

Those who bypass these requirements and seek rebirth in the Pure Land by reciting the Buddha’s name are like those who receive hereditary rank or promotions based on their ancestors' service; they rely on the power of others and do not depend on whether they have cultivated their own studies.

This is also like a general amnesty that universally promotes all officials; the merit derives from the King, regardless of the depth or brevity of their prior service. In such cases, the horizontal leap does not depend on one's own qualifications.

Because there are both concentrated and distracted forms of wholesome practice within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the Venerable Master Shandao established the two modes of cultivation—exclusive and miscellaneous—as seen in the preceding text;
those who act according to this find that there is no lack of efficacy (as recorded in the *Lèbāng wénlèi*).
Master Lun of Mount Tang said: "The various Mahāyāna sūtras encourage birth in the Pure Land through two types of causes: one is concentrated (samādhi) and the other is dispersed (vikṣepa).

'Concentrated' means that one contemplates the Buddha within one's own mind. One visualizes the environment and inhabitants, the primary and secondary aspects of the Western Land, as being inherently complete within the mind.
Because my mind is empty, the Tathāgata is fundamentally empty; because my mind is provisional, the Tathāgata is vividly present within my mind."
The Tathāgata is beyond all dependence; imagine a lotus flower opening and closing, and I dwell within it.

The closing represents emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the opening represents the conventional (*prajñapti*), and the identity of the four subtle elements (*catur-mahābhūta*) represents the Middle Way. Thus, the Sūtra says: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the Dharma-realm body;
they enter into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings. Therefore, when you contemplate the Buddha in your mind, that mind is itself..."

These thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics are created by this mind; this mind is the Buddha. This is the Tathāgata’s personal revelation of the Samādhi of Mind-Only, the essence of the perfect and eternal contemplation.
One realizes that the pure land, the Buddhas, the environment and its inhabitants, and both form and mind are all the substance of my own mind-nature.
Since the mind inherently possesses all merit, the objective realm itself becomes the contemplative mind; outside the mind there is no Buddha, and outside the nature there is nothing.

First, by contemplating the absence of [intrinsic] substance without ceasing, one realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Second, regarding the practice of scattering [the mind], it is beneficial to employ a pure and sincere heart, believing in the Western Land and maintaining single-mindedness without distraction.
One should fix the mindfulness on Amitābha for one or seven days, with every sound uninterrupted and every thought continuous.
As the Sūtra says: "If one upholds the Name for one or seven days with a single mind and without distraction, when that person’s life ends..."
Amitābha Buddha and the assembly of holy beings now stand before one;

yet, while the visualization of that land involves only the "scattered good" (dispersed virtues) as it lacks the three contemplations, the dedication of the three types of pure karma with the vow to be born there ensures that all shall ascend to Sukhāvatī. Our Patriarch Zhiyi said:
"Roots have sharpness or dullness, and practices have concentration or dispersion. The samādhi of visualizing the Buddha is called 'concentrated cultivation,' while other virtues are 'dispersed.'"
It is said that karma is "scattered" (dispersed), and scattered wholesome roots are weak and cannot eliminate the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*).

This sutra clarifies that through contemplation, one attains rebirth in the Pure Land. Thus we know that whether in a state of concentration or distraction, and whether dull or sharp, all are causes for the Pure Land;
they all proceed toward non-arising (*anutpāda*) and shall never again fall back. (The Method of Cultivating the Mind through Buddha-Recitation)
The Dharma Master Simfan asked: "In the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*, it is taught that one should bring Amitābha Buddha to mind in every thought-moment;
this implies that the mind possesses mental objects (*saṃjñā*). Yet, later in the same sūtra, it states: 'If the mind has mental objects, there is delusion;

if the mind has no mental objects, that is nirvāṇa. How can these two preceding and succeeding passages be mutually contradictory? He replied: "That sūtra first clarifies that when contemplating and visualizing Amitābha, one must not be without mindfulness (*smṛti*); subsequently..."
When the merit of samādhi is perfected, one sees the Buddhas of the ten directions standing in the air;

at this time, one should realize that one's own mind and the Buddha-mind are identical within the single true nature and are inconceivable. Therefore it is said: "To have thoughts is delusion; to be without thoughts is nirvāṇa.
This does not mean that from the very beginning one must not practice contemplation. Furthermore, the wisdom of non-thought and non-arising is the stage of Buddhahood.

To claim that people today have not yet entered the gate of contemplative practice and can nonetheless speak of non-arising and non-thought—how could they know that what Asvaghosa taught was to proceed from thought to no-thought, and from speech to no-speech? The Mañjuśrī-prajñā Sūtra states:
"It is like a person learning archery; through long practice they become skillful, such that later, even though they have no conscious intent, every arrow they release hits the mark. If a person...

"Entering the Samādhi of One Practice by single-mindedly reciting the name, with mindfulness succeeding mindfulness without interruption, one will see the Buddhas of the ten directions within that very mindfulness.
This shows that using mindfulness to still mindfulness and using words to dispel words is the correct path for the practice of the Buddhas and Patriarchs" (Huizong ji).
One day, a student asked Chan Master Haihui, "I wish to be reborn in the Pure Land; I wonder if such a Pure Land truly exists. The Master replied, "The sutras state:
'If you wish to attain a pure land, you must purify your mind. As the mind becomes pure, so too does the Buddha-land become pure.
If the mind is pure, wherever one dwells is a pure land. It is like being born as a king's son."
One who is determined to succeed to the royal foundation and resolves their mind toward the Buddha-way will be born in a pure buddha-land;
if that mind is not pure, then wherever they are born, it is all a defiled land. Purity and defilement reside in the mind, not in the land.
(Fengfa Chengyuan Lu)
Master Yuanbian said: "The Pure Land of the Mind is but one.

This is truly because Amitābha realized that my own mind is the precious land, and my own mind possesses the blissful realm of Amitābha. Though distant, it is near, not departing from a single thought;

though near, it is distant, exceeding ten million *koṭis* of lands. It is like the bright moon in a clear blue sky, its reflection appearing upon all waters, yet the water does not [contain the moon]."
"The rising moon does not descend; the moon reflected in water is of one essence, naturally illuminating and reflecting" (*Bǎozhū jí*).

Jishì said: "To let the mind roam in meditative concentration and awaken to the principle of the nature of things—when such a person is shown the Pure Land, they must say that the Pure Land is but the mind.
If my own mind is pure, then the land is pure; why then seek another place of rebirth elsewhere? Now, let us ask this again. And so forth.
In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the Tathāgata pressed the earth with his toe, and the Sahā world was seen to be entirely adorned and pure;
yet while the assembled multitude did not see it, only the Brahma King Śikhin perceived it. Can those who practice dhyāna today perceive the Pure Land as clearly as the Brahma King Śikhin?
How much more so should you, who dwell in humble rooms and dilapidated houses, envy them for grand mansions and lofty palaces!
If one eats coarse grain and millet soup in the hall, yet envies delicacies and sweet flavors;
or if one wears tattered robes and coarse cloth, yet envies patterned silks and fine gauze—if this is what you mean by "purity of mind," then it does not eliminate the aforementioned discriminations.

Moreover, at a time when the world is beset by the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, if one’s outward appearance is no different from that of those who have not yet awakened, then one is merely chanting with the mouth.
To say that while the mind is pure the land is pure, yet one’s own body remains bound by the afflictions of this defiled world, is the height of self-deception.

Otherwise, one must believe the teachings and rely on principle; within the single gate of the Pure Land, one should choose the virtuous path and cultivate it accordingly (as seen in the *Lèbāng wénlèi*).
When worldly people practice pure karma, they must not say: "I am busy now, so I will wait until I have leisure;
I am destitute now, so I will wait until I am wealthy; I am young and strong now, so I will wait until old age.

If one's lot is fixed such that one is constantly busy, one's lot is fixed in poverty, or one's lot is fixed for an early death, then there will be no opportunity to cultivate pure karma, and one will suddenly perish. Even if...
What use is regret once it is too late? Therefore, I exhort all people: you should strive to practice now, while this body is still healthy and strong.
Worldly people know only to nourish and provide for this body during their lifetime, yet they do not consider abandoning it.
Since the consciousness does not perish, if one lacks virtuous causes, one will fall into the paths of suffering.
Why is it that while you cherish this body during life, you do not think to rescue and deliver that very same mind after death?
Furthermore, worldly people devote themselves exclusively to providing food and clothing for their wives, children, male and female servants, and kinsmen, never failing in the slightest effort; yet—
Reflect upon the time of death: though one's wife, children, and grandchildren may love one with a depth that penetrates to the very marrow of the bones, they cannot provide mutual rescue;
one must go forth alone. I now exhort people of the world: you should not, for the sake of sustaining life, forget the fear of death;
nor should you, for the sake of others, forget what is for your own self.
Yang Cigong’s *Preface to the Ten Doubts on Tiantai* states in brief: "If love is not profound, one will not be born in Saṃsāra;
if mindfulness is not singular, one will not be born in Sukhāvatī. Saṃsāra is the defiled land, while Sukhāvatī is the pure land.
The lifespan in Saṃsāra is finite, whereas the lifespan in that land is infinite. Saṃsāra is replete with all sufferings, while that land is one of peaceful nourishment, free from suffering."

In this Sahā world, beings revolve through birth and death according to their karma; yet in that land, one attains the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) upon first arrival.
If one wishes to save sentient beings, one acts with sovereign freedom, no longer driven by various karmic forces.

While there are such differences between purity and defilement, the duration of life, suffering and joy, and birth and death, sentient beings remain in profound ignorance of these distinctions—is this not lamentable?
(From the *Asaṃskṛta-samuccaya*). It is further said:
"The light of Amitābha pervades the entire Dharma-realm; he embraces and does not abandon those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

The holy and the ordinary are of one essence, as the resonance between the capacity [of the practitioner] and the response [of the Buddha] occurs. Sentient beings within the minds of all Buddhas are each and every atom of the Land of Ultimate Bliss; the minds of sentient beings are [themselves] the Land of Ultimate Bliss."
In the Middle Pure Land, Amitābha is present in every thought-moment; observing this, those with wisdom find it easy to be born there because they can sever doubt;

those in meditative concentration find it easy to be born there because they are not distracted; those who uphold the precepts find it easy to be born there because they remain far removed from defilements;

those who practice giving find it easy to be born there because they have no sense of "mine"; those who practice patience find it easy to be born there because they harbor no anger; and those who practice diligence...
Because it is easy to give rise to non-retrogression; because those who do not create good nor commit evil easily give rise to pure and single-minded mindfulness;
and because those for whom the karma of past evils has already manifested as retribution easily give rise to genuine shame and dread.
Even if one possesses many virtues, if one lacks sincere faith, lacks a profound mind, and lacks the mind of dedication and aspiration, one shall not attain birth in the highest of the high grades.
Alas! Amitābha is exceedingly easy to invoke, and the Pure Land is exceedingly easy to reach. That sentient beings cannot invoke him or go there—what does this say of the Buddha toward these beings?
To create evil karma and enter the realms of suffering, and to recite the name of Amitābha and be born in the Ultimate Bliss—both of these are words of the Buddha.
Is it not a delusion for worldly people to fear falling into hell while doubting rebirth in the Pure Land?
The *Preface to the Collection for Resolving Doubts Concerning Direct Pointing to the Pure Land* states in brief: "The Sage of Great Vows comes from the Pure Land, yet his coming is truly no coming;
ordinary beings of deep resolve go to the Pure Land, yet their going is truly no going.
That he does not come here and they do not go there, and yet the Sage and the ordinary being meet and achieve communion—how is this so? It is because Amitābha’s light is like..."

The great full moon shines universally upon the waters of the ten directions: when the water is clear and still, the moon appears in its entirety; yet the moon does not hasten to the water from elsewhere.
When the water is turbid and moving, the moon lacks its steady radiance; yet the moon does not abandon the water to depart suddenly.

While clarity and turbidity, movement and stillness exist within the water, there is no grasping or rejecting, no coming or going within the moon. Thus, it is said in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "Liberation."
The Elder said: "Know that all Buddhas are like reflections and one's own mind is like water.
Those Tathāgatas do not come here, nor do I go there. If I wish to see the Tathāgata Amitābha of the Land of Peace and Bliss, I shall see him at will.
Thus it is known that when sentient beings focus their mindfulness with concentration, they see Amitābha; Amitābha comes to welcome them to Sukhāvatī."
It is not far from the truth to say that this refers to the words of ultimate reality and is not a provisional teaching.
Furthermore, it is said: "There are virtuous people in the world who give rise to three kinds of faithless thoughts and do not seek rebirth [in the Pure Land], which is all the more lamentable.
The first is: 'I shall transcend the Buddhas and surpass the Patriarchs; the Pure Land is not a place where I need to be born. The second is: 'Every place is pure.'"
It is not that one will necessarily be born in the Western Quarter; thirdly, it is said that the Holy Realm of Ultimate Bliss cannot be reached by us ordinary beings.
Yet, the ocean of practice is inexhaustible, and the vows of Samantabhadra lead one to behold the Land of Amitābha Buddha.

Although that land is empty, Vimalakīrti constantly cultivates the Pure Land, and the Tathāgatas of the ten directions offer praise with their broad tongues, while the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions share the resolve to go there together.
Try to reflect for yourself: how do you compare with the various sages? To say that one is unworthy of being born [in the Pure Land]—how is this self-deception!

As for the patriarch Nāgārjuna, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* contains a prophetic record of him; as for Vasubandhu, the founder of the Yogācāra school, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* contains verses on seeking birth [there].
When Master Ci'en (Xuanzang) praised him in his *Commentary on the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, he first extolled his "ten superior wisdoms," analyzing the principles with clarity and discernment.

To harbor ten doubts regarding those who were all eminent sages and diligent practitioners who attained rebirth in the Pure Land—claiming they need not have been born there—is nothing short of self-contempt.

The fire chariots of hell can be extinguished; the boat with the stone will not sink. Among those who manifest immediate karmic rewards (*vipāka*), none surpass Zhang Kui, who transcended to the supreme realm through ten recitations.
Among those who enter hell, none do so more swiftly than Xiong Jun, who was revived and realized the wondrous cause. Such is the case for the people of this world.
That transgressions and faults are not necessarily as such—that one cannot be reborn—is how can one call this self-abandonment?
To deceive oneself, to be self-disrespectful, and to abandon one’s own spiritual nature, thereby flowing into the cycle of saṃsāra—whose fault is this?
When Elder Chen discussed the Three Thousand Dharmas of the Tiantai school with Dharma Master Mingzhi, he explained the meaning of the Pure Land of the Mind-only, saying:
"When a single thought arises, the three thousand natures and characteristics arise simultaneously; when a single thought ceases, the three thousand natures and characteristics cease simultaneously.
Outside of this thought, not even a hair’s breadth of a dharma can be found; outside of dharmas, not even a hair’s breadth of a thought can be found."
Having attained this Dharma of the unchanging nature of reality, wherein the essence of the perfect clarity of principle serves as its life-force, its lifespan is immeasurable;
it is not a life-root obtained through karmic retribution, nor is there any continuity to maintain it. Originally devoid of names, yet it does not reject various designations:
its land is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī) and its body is named "Amitābha. Body and land interpenetrate and merge in harmony.
Within this single wondrous capacity for preaching the Dharma, the sound does not leave that land, yet the mark of the broad and long tongue is fully present and all-pervasive.
That which is thus equipped—is it the essence? Is it the Buddha who possesses it? Is it sentient beings who possess it? Or is it empty?
If there were anyone capable of knowing the joy of possessing that, would they not wish to be reborn there? This is directed toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The essential point therein is to "go" without actually going within the sphere of skillful means; what harm is there in having gone and then returning?
When the capacity is matured and the resonance is deep, it is sufficient that the task be accomplished.
The *Liaozhai ji* states: "In Chao Shuo zhi’s letter responding to Zhao He zi, it is briefly said that while there is birth and death, ordinary beings and sages..."
There is a profound distinction between the ordinary and the holy, for body and land differ. Where there is a body, there is a land;
where there is a land, there is a body. Who is defiled and who is pure? How can this not be discerned?

Out of compassion for these sentient beings, our Śākyamuni Buddha and Amitābha Buddha have, through a single power of aspiration, established this [Pure Land] beyond the measureless and boundless gates of the Dharma.
In this single Dharma-gate, Śākyamuni acts as the guest while Amitābha presides as the host; Śākyamuni brings one forth, while Amitābha provides a home.
Śākyamuni administers medicine for the illness, while Amitābha ensures that one remains forever free from illness.
The land of Śākyamuni is like a transient inn, whereas the land of Amitābha is like one’s native village—so it is when gazing back from Western India.
"The Land of Peace and Bliss and our own land of Zhendan—our aspiration for the Land of Peace and Bliss is one and the same" (as seen in the *Lebang wenlei*).
Master Jiang Gongwang said: "For those of keen faculties, in every thought-moment nothing arises;

the mind has no object, the six sense-faculties are profoundly still, and the various consciousnesses dissolve away. Every dharma is entirely true, and every gate is free from dependence. In a mere flash, they achieve the true contemplation of reality."
For beginners and those newly studying, one may temporarily suspend mindfulness only during times of greeting guests with pleasantries,
or when attending to the needs of nature; otherwise, unless one cannot yet abstain from pungent foods, or while sleeping until deep sleep has arrived,
or while performing various household chores and tasks, one should not abandon it, nor will it interfere with such activities, as one should recite the name with every thought and every word.
What further evil thoughts or malicious intentions could dare to sprout within the mind of one who possesses such a sacred name? Naturally, they become pure and singular without admixture.
If one can fully restrain the six sense faculties and maintain a succession of pure mindfulness, then within ten days or a month, one will achieve samādhi.

This is what is meant by "this mind makes the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha. Those of superior capacity and great potential transcend directly in a single thought-moment; those of ordinary, gradual disposition must proceed through diligent cultivation.
On the Expedient Means of Contemplation (The Text on the Expedient Means of Mindfulness of the Buddha).

Huang Yue said: "In antiquity, those who were driven by a heart of dread shot arrows that pierced stone; those whose fierce indignation was intense caused mountains to split and springs to gush forth.
If such sincerity arising from within can move even insentient things, how much more so when one tears asunder the net of doubt and consolidates the root of faith!"
Through the samādhi of buddha-remembrance, if one practices with unwavering diligence, one will certainly attain birth in the Pure Land despite its distance (Epilogue to the *Ten Doubts*).
Wang Rixiu said: "While it is truly supreme to achieve great enlightenment through Zen meditation and thereby escape the cycle of birth and death, those who reach such a state are likely few.
If one cultivates the Western Paradise, however, one directly cuts off the cycle of rebirth without a single failure; therefore, I now exhort [you to do so]."

For those who practice Chan meditation, if they set aside even a brief moment each day to cultivate the Western Pure Land, and if they should achieve great awakening and transcend the cycle of birth and death, it would still be far from reaching the Buddha-ground;
what, then, could be improper about going further to see Amitābha Buddha, prostrating and paying homage?
Even for those who have not yet attained great penetration and awakening, when their lifespan suddenly comes to an end, they shall go directly to the West to behold him.

If the Buddha hears the Dharma, how could he fail to attain great enlightenment? If one does not cultivate the Western Pure Land, one cannot avoid receiving various retributions according to one's karma. (Longshu Jingtu Wen)

To practice *chan* meditation in pursuit of great enlightenment while refusing to cultivate the Western Paradise is like a person who, having attained the rank of a minor official, refuses to accept it and instead insists on studying for the highest imperial degree (*da kuai*).
Such an ambition is indeed noble; however, the highest degree cannot be guaranteed.
It would be better to first accept the official post and then devote oneself to study. If one subsequently attains the highest degree, it is like adding embroidery to brocade. If not...
"To attain and not lose one's status as an official" refers to those who cultivate the Western Pure Land and receive a single office.

"Cultivating learning on one side while simultaneously engaging in Chan" refers to this very practice. "Not attaining the Grand Champion (the highest degree)" refers to one whose Chan practice has not yet reached enlightenment.
"Not losing one's status as an official" is a direct explanation of the cycle of saṃsāra. Having been born in the Western Pure Land...
Are there those who do not attain great awakening? It is like a person entering a great city who must first seek a place to settle before going out to attend to their business;
when evening falls and it becomes dark, they will have a place to lodge. Seeking a place to settle first is what is meant by cultivating the Pure Land.
When evening falls and it becomes dark is what is meant by the arrival of one’s great destiny. Having a place to lodge...
The phrase "the place" refers to being born within a lotus flower and not falling into the evil realms. Furthermore, it is like traveling a long distance during the spring months:
one must first prepare for rain; if a sudden downpour occurs, one will suffer no distress from getting soaked.
Preparing for the rain beforehand is what is meant by cultivating the Pure Land. A sudden downpour occurring is what is meant by the imminent end of one's life. To be without distress...
The fear of the Li River refers to the state of not falling into the evil realms to undergo suffering.
Furthermore, one who first seeks a place to settle does not hinder their management of affairs; one who prepares for rain does not hinder their long journey.
Thus, those who cultivate the Pure Land do not obstruct any worldly duties. Why, then, would anyone not practice it?
They made offerings to the Buddhas, provided meals for the Sangha, constructed stupas and monasteries, and engaged in recitation and repentance.

They were filial toward their parents and fraternal toward their siblings; among their clans and kin, there was no lack of harmony. Toward their fellow villagers and neighbors, they exchanged kindness and courtesy. When serving their sovereign, they offered their sincere hearts for the sake of the state;

when serving as officials, they were benevolent and compassionate for the benefit of the people. When acting as leaders, they governed well to bring peace to the masses; when serving as subordinates, they...
Diligently serve superiors; instruct the ignorant and deluded; assist the solitary and the weak; rescue those in urgent distress; bestow gifts upon the poor;
construct bridges and lay wells; distribute food and dispense medicine; reduce one’s own provisions for dependents to benefit others;
when encountering wealth, give generously while reflecting upon oneself; teach others to do good; and protect and preserve virtue.

Regarding evil, one merely follows what is done; however, for all worldly and world-transcending wholesome deeds, regardless of whether they are small or great, few or many—whether it be giving a single coin to another or using a single drop of water to quench thirst—even down to the slightest virtue of a hair’s breadth—one must give rise to the thought:
"May these virtuous conditions be dedicated toward the Western Land. If this mindful intention is uninterrupted, one will certainly be reborn in the highest grade.
The Great King of Physicians can cure all diseases, yet he cannot cure one whose life has reached its end;
the Buddha can deliver all sentient beings, yet he cannot deliver those who lack faith. To compare the lack of faith with the exhaustion of one's life is the ultimate analogy.
A person of good faith possesses even a single thought; if a person, while still alive, has the mental resolve to depart, their body will follow accordingly.
If the mind intends to go while the body remains, the body will follow wherever it dwells; this is what is meant by "constant mindfulness of the body.
There are also those who intend to go but whose bodies are bound and restrained; yet at the moment of death, there is only a single thought.

Therefore, if one possesses a single thought of the Pure Land, one will certainly take rebirth within a lotus flower—how much more so when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas beckon and lead one forth through their great vows!

Wang Zhonghui asked Yang Ci, "How can one ensure that mindfulness is never interrupted? Ci replied, "Once faith is established, never again to doubt—this is precisely what it means for mindfulness to be uninterrupted.
Zhonghui agreed with his words and applied himself even more diligently to the practice of Pure Land cultivation.

Since there is no phenomenon outside of mind, it is called "Mind-Only. This very dharma of mind is metaphorically named "Pure Land," yet this dharma of mind cannot be apprehended.
The mental dharmas are vividly present, yet they mutually vanish and mutually persist; beyond thought and beyond discourse, the sages and scholars of antiquity wondrously attained this state.
When there is neither Buddha nor the state of non-thought, they constantly cultivate the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance with fervent diligence;

by the natural law of things, they are all reborn in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. This tradition dates back to ancient times. However, later students cling to their own emotions and give rise to attachments, falling into a biased view of emptiness.

Seeing those who have fallen into the pit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), who cling to the state where there is no Buddha and no objects of mindfulness as being "dead words," who fail to attain their wondrous function,
who do not believe the Buddha’s words, and who seek neither liberation nor find sweetness in the long eons of saṃsāra within the five turbidities—

the Tathāgata calls them objects of compassion. This Master Daoci set out his journey from the traditions of Tiantai and Jingxiu, investigated the mind through the "Direct Pointing" (*zhízhǐ*), and extensively synthesized [the various teachings].
While broadly mastering the inner scriptures and the hundred schools during the prime of my life when I was practicing the Way, I have devoted my whole heart and will to this path;
could there not be some attainment herein? Furthermore, sighing that this path might benefit many people, I have thus composed this *Jìngtǔ Jiǎnyàolù* (A Brief Record of the Pure Land).
As this book circulates throughout the ten directions, each of the countless Buddhas of the *gāṅgā-nadī-vāluka* sands shall extend their broad [hands].
With a long tongue, he speaks words of sincerity; with a single voice, he offers praise. How could this be merely the empty sky nodding its head and the myriad phenomena appreciating the sound?
